meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Charity is no substitute for justice withheld'?
meta.ogDescription: Widely credited to Augustine, but no work of his contains it. The trail starts in a 1957 book by columnist Sydney J. Harris.

answer.label: Not Augustine of Hippo — unsourced wording
answer.authorDates: 354–430 · Bishop of Hippo; no known source for this line
answer.sourceLine: No work of Augustine’s has been found that contains this sentence. Wikiquote ↗ files it under Disputed and cites only Sydney J. Harris’s 1957 book Majority of One, where the line is introduced simply with “Augustine remarked.” The words’ true origin is unknown.

source.heading: Where the line actually appears

docMeta.dd: Sydney J. Harris (Chicago Daily News columnist)

source.excerpt: Augustine remarked: “Charity is no substitute for justice withheld.”
trail: Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in Augustine’s Disputed section. Its only citation is “Majority of One (1957) by Sydney J. Harris, p. 283.”
Harris’s Majority of One (Houghton Mifflin, 1957) ↗ is a collection of his newspaper columns. It introduces the line with “Augustine remarked” and, in the indexed passage, names no work.

After 1957 the line spreads through books on social teaching and then through general quotation books. An Internet Archive full-text search ↗ turns up the 1983 Barnes & Noble Book of Quotations and many later anthologies, almost always signed “St. Augustine.”

The closest genuine Augustine text makes a different point: “You give bread to the hungry: but better it were that none hungered, and you had none to give to.” It comes from Homily 8 on the First Epistle of John, §5 ↗, in H. Browne’s 1888 translation.
source.excerptNote: This is the passage as the Internet Archive’s full-text index shows it in Harris’s Majority of One (1957). The indexed passage names no work by Augustine. Wikiquote gives the page as p. 283.
source.rightsNote: The sentence’s author is unknown, and it is not in any of Augustine’s works, so we assert no rights status for the words themselves. The earliest book we found carrying them, Sydney J. Harris’s Majority of One (1957), is a 1931-or-later publication and should be treated as in copyright.

author.name: Augustine of Hippo
author.heading: About Augustine of Hippo
author.metaLine: 354–430 · Bishop of Hippo Regius, theologian & philosopher
author.bio: Augustine was bishop of Hippo Regius in Roman North Africa. He wrote the Confessions, The City of God and On the Trinity. He did write about almsgiving and need. In his eighth homily on the First Epistle of John he says, “You give bread to the hungry: but better it were that none hungered, and you had none to give to.” But the tidy line about “justice withheld” has not been found anywhere in his writings.

misattribution.heading: Why Augustine gets the credit
misattribution.intro: The line sounds like a Church Father, and Augustine is the internet’s default author for moral one-liners. Every trail we followed leads back to a mid-twentieth-century book, not to Augustine’s Latin.

items.why: The sentence has not been located in any of Augustine’s works. Wikiquote ↗ lists it as Disputed, and its only source is a 1957 secondary book.

Harris, a columnist, printed the line in Majority of One (1957) ↗ as something “Augustine remarked.” He did not claim it as his own, and nothing shows he coined it. It is simply the earliest printing we found.

General quotation books, starting with the 1983 Barnes & Noble Book of Quotations, repeat the line as “St. Augustine” without citing a work. You can see this in an Internet Archive full-text search ↗. That repetition is what spread the credit online.

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody knows who first wrote these exact words. The trail runs back to Sydney J. Harris’s 1957 Majority of One, which credits Augustine without naming a work, and Wikiquote ↗ keeps it under Disputed.

context.heading: Why it caught on
lead: The line has been used for decades in arguments about charity and social reform: almsgiving cannot make up for unjust structures. Augustine’s name gives the slogan ancient authority. That authority is borrowed. The words do not appear in his writings.

Augustine did write on the theme. He told his listeners that it would be better if no one were hungry at all than to keep handing out bread (Homily 8 on 1 John ↗). But that is a remark about love and need, not a maxim about justice withheld.
